summary: One run tried many ports on one host, or many hosts, within minutes, and sent nothing to them.

thresholds_explained.window_ms: How close together the probes must start to count as one scan (5 minutes). A tool reaching twenty services over a day is not scanning.
thresholds_explained.ports_on_one_host: Distinct ports on one address, each connected to and sent no data, that make a port scan (20). Ordinary software talks to a handful of ports on any one host.
thresholds_explained.hosts: Distinct addresses, each connected to and sent no data, that make a host sweep (20). A package install reaches many hosts too, but it sends a request to every one, so those are not probes.

probe_note: A probe is a destination the run connected to, or tried to, and wrote no bytes to. Name lookups (port 53) and the port-0 connects a resolver makes to rank addresses are never probes. Outcome is reported, not required: a scanner using non-blocking connects sees most attempts as 'in progress', so 'mostly failing' cannot be the test.

card.name: Network Scanning
why: A coding agent connects to its model service, package registries and the hosts a task names. Trying many ports or many addresses without sending anything is how a network is mapped before an attack.
It sent no data to any of them: it was checking what answers, not using a service.
actions: Stop the program and check what task it was given.
Check the addresses it reached: an answer on an unexpected port is a service it may try next.
limits: Topgent counts connection attempts and bytes written. It does not see packets, so a raw-socket (SYN) scan that bypasses connect is not counted.
A slow scan spread over hours, a few ports at a time, stays under the 5-minute window.
A program that legitimately checks many hosts, such as a monitoring or discovery tool, raises this too; the card names the program.
